1.note: The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

Here, **name** represents who Yahweh is or to refer to Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [praise everything about Yahweh]

2.note: The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [We bless Yahweh] or [Let us all praise Yahweh]

The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Let us bless the name of Yahweh]

The psalmist is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is or to refer to Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Blessed be Yahweh]

The psalmist is referring to all of time by naming two extremes, **now** and **to forever**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for all eternity]

3.note: The psalmist is referring to all of the earth by naming two extremes, **the rising of the sun** and **its setting**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [All over the earth]

The expression **may the name of Yahweh be praised** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [may people praise the name of Yahweh]

Here, **name** represents who Yahweh is or to refer to Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [may Yahweh be praised] or [may everything about Yahweh be praised]

4.note: Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were physically **high above** the nations, like someone standing on a mountain looking down. This image emphasizes Yahweh’s supreme authority and power over all earthly kingdoms. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is supreme over all nations]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [his glory is high above the skies]

Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh’s **glory** as if it were positioned **above the skies**. The psalmist means that Yahweh’s glory is greater than anything that can be seen in the heavens. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his glory exceeds anything visible from earth]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he is more glorious than anything visible from earth]

5.note: The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis, which begins here and continues through verse 6. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no one like Yahweh our God]

The psalmist is using **the one making high to sit** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the one who sits on high” or “the one who rules in the highest position.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one sitting on high] or [the one who rules in the highest position]

6.note: This is the second part of the question form that began in verse 5. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for the purpose of creating emphasis as this does, you could translate these two verses as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [the one making low to look on the sky and on the earth.]

The psalmist is using **the one making low to look** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the one who humbles himself to look” or “the one who condescends to look.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who lowers himself to look down on the sky and on the earth]

7.q: מְקִֽימִ֣י מֵ⁠עָפָ֣ר דָּ֑ל מֵֽ֝⁠אַשְׁפֹּ֗ת יָרִ֥ים אֶבְיֽוֹן
7.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [raising up the poor from the dust, yes, he lifts the needy from the garbage]

7.q: מְקִֽימִ֣י מֵ⁠עָפָ֣ר דָּ֑ל מֵֽ֝⁠אַשְׁפֹּ֗ת יָרִ֥ים אֶבְיֽוֹן
7.note: Here the psalmist is speaking of the extremely poor condition of needy people as if they were sitting in **dust** and **garbage**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he takes the poor out of their dirty and poor condition]

7.q: מְקִֽימִ֣י מֵ⁠עָפָ֣ר דָּ֑ל מֵֽ֝⁠אַשְׁפֹּ֗ת יָרִ֥ים אֶבְיֽוֹן
7.note: The psalmist is using the adjectives **poor** and **needy** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [raising up poor people from the dust, he lifts needy people from the garbage]

8.note: The psalmist is using **to seat him with princes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to give him a position of honor and authority.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to cause him to rule with princes]
The pronoun **him** refers to the poor person mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to seat the poor person with princes]

The phrase **with the princes of his people** clarifies who the princes are from the previous phrase. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [that is, to seat him with the princes of his people]
Here, **his** could refer to: (1) Yahweh. Alternate translation: [with the princes of Yahweh’s people] or (2) the poor person. Alternate translation: [with the princes of the man’s people]

9.note: The implication is that God transforms a barren woman into a mother by giving her children. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He causes a woman who is barren to become the joyful mother of children]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **barren woman**. He means barren women in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [He causes barren women of their houses to dwell]

The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]
